chapterTitle: Arrays and Pointers: A Close Relationship
aiGenerationNote: Develop a 12-minute interactive code demo focusing on arrays and pointers. Start with a visual representation of an array `int data[5]` in memory, showing each element's value and address. Animate how `data[i]` directly maps to `*(data + i)`. Allow the user to input an index `i` and see the corresponding element highlighted and its value displayed, both through array indexing and pointer arithmetic. Demonstrate the "array decay" concept by showing a function call `myFunction(data, size)` where `data` transforms into a simple pointer `int *arr_param` in the function's scope, and explain why `sizeof(arr_param)` inside the function is different. Include a small coding exercise where learners complete a function to calculate the average of array elements using pointer arithmetic. Provide clear visual warnings about accessing memory out of bounds.

screens.title: Arrays and Pointers: A Close Relationship
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will develop an intuitive picture of arrays and pointers in C and why they are tightly linked. Arrays are contiguous memory: elements sit next to each other so the address of one element directly leads to the next. That layout makes pointer arithmetic meaningful because moving a pointer moves by an element size, not by single bytes. You will learn the practical equivalence where an array name used in expressions becomes a pointer to its first element, what that decay means for assigning and for function calls, and why sizeof can mislead when used inside a function parameter. Along the way we will practice two ways to access elements — indexing and pointer arithmetic — and write small functions that accept arrays safely by receiving a pointer and a length. Finally, we will cover a critical safety topic: buffer overflows, why they happen when code writes past an array's bounds, and safer alternatives such as bounded copy functions. By the end you will be able to read and write array code with clearer expectations about addresses, performance, and safety, and answer practical questions such as why passing an array to a function does not copy all elements.

In this lesson

Array decay and passing to functions.
Safety

Why this matters

Efficient array access underpins many core algorithms. Knowing how pointer arithmetic maps to element addresses helps you reason about performance, interoperability with C APIs, and prevents mistakes when memory is read or written incorrectly. The decay behavior explains common surprises when measuring sizes inside functions.

Writing past the allocated element count corrupts nearby memory and can cause crashes or security issues.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will understand arrays as contiguous memory that stores elements of the same type, and you will be able to explain how array names commonly decay into pointers to their first element. You will learn to access elements with both array indexing and pointer arithmetic, and you will practice passing arrays to functions while correctly handling sizes because arrays decay into pointers at call sites. Finally, you will be able to identify and prevent common array-related errors, especially buffer overflows, by using bounds checks and safer library calls. For example, you will explain why giving a function just an array parameter does not preserve its original size and why you must pass a separate length. These skills let you write safer, clearer code that interoperates correctly with C APIs, and they form a foundation for working with multidimensional arrays and low-level memory reasoning.

screens.title: Arrays as Contiguous Memory
screens.narratorSegment: An array is a fixed-size collection where elements of the same type occupy adjacent memory locations. Contiguous means no gaps: the address of element i plus one equals the address of element i plus the size of each element. That property is what enables efficient iteration, pointer arithmetic, and predictable address computation. For example, for an int array of five elements the compiler lays out five integer-sized slots in order so moving forward by one slot means advancing by the size of int on your platform. A common misconception is to treat an array name as a general-purpose pointer variable you can reassign; in C an array name often converts to a pointer in expressions but it is not a modifiable lvalue and cannot be assigned a new address. Another practical point: because memory is contiguous, traversing arrays with pointer arithmetic or indexing yields identical machine behavior, and the compiler can optimize linear scans effectively. Concrete example: if you declare int numbers[5]; the element numbers[3] resides at the address computed from numbers plus three times sizeof(int). Why this matters: understanding contiguity helps you predict performance, avoid accidental aliasing errors, and reason about how multi-dimensional arrays map to memory in row-major order. Try visualizing memory addresses as numbered slots; that mental model reveals how indexing and pointer math match perfectly.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Contiguous storage means array elements are adjacent, enabling simple address arithmetic and efficient traversal.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Arrays: Contiguous
Contiguous memory explains addresses
Elements are placed next to each other so address arithmetic is predictable.
Conceptual memory slots (int numbers[5])
[0] value 85
addr 0x100
[1] value 92
addr 0x104
[2] value 78
addr 0x108
[3] value 95
addr 0x10C
[4] value 88
addr 0x110
Bullets
  • Contiguity means adjacent addresses equal element offsets times the element size.
  • Pointer arithmetic moves by element size automatically.
  • Compilers can optimize linear scans thanks to predictable layout.
Example
If numbers is at address 0x100 on a system with 4-byte ints, numbers + 3 will point to 0x10C, the start of numbers[3].
Key Takeaway

Think of arrays as numbered slots so address arithmetic becomes simple multiplication by element size.

Common misconception
An array name is not an assignable pointer variable. It will act like a pointer in many expressions, but you cannot reassign the array name to point elsewhere.
Why this helps
Predict memory accesses, avoid undefined behavior from invalid pointer arithmetic, and reason about multi-dimensional layouts which are also contiguous in row-major order.

screens.title: Pointer Arithmetic Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Pointer arithmetic means the unit of pointer movement is the size of the pointed type. When you add one to an int pointer you advance by the number of bytes in an int on that platform. This behavior lets pointer expressions compute the address of any element: pointer plus index yields the correct memory location scaled by the element size. For example, if p points to an int array start, then p plus two points to the third int. A typical misunderstanding is thinking pointer addition moves by single bytes; it does not. The compiler scales the offset by sizeof(the pointed type). This scaling is what makes constructs like p plus i portable across platforms with different primitive sizes. Another practical note: you can both dereference the result of pointer addition and use indexing syntax — arr[i] is shorthand for *(arr + i). That identity helps you rewrite code for clarity or to practice pointer traversal in low-level loops. Example: walking a scores array with a loop that increments a pointer until it reaches the end uses the same element orders and yields identical values to an indexed loop. A closing question to try: if you have a pointer to row zero of a two-dimensional array, what does pointer plus one represent in terms of columns and rows?

keyIdea.title: Process
keyIdea.text: Adding to a pointer advances by the pointed type's size; arr[i] equals *(arr + i).

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Pointer Arithmetic
Pointer arithmetic scales by type size
The compiler interprets pointer addition as an increase by element size, not single bytes.
Step-by-step
  1. Start with pointer p pointing to element 0.
  2. Compute p + i: compiler multiplies i by sizeof(*p).
  3. Dereference *(p + i) to access element i.
Concrete example
If p points to address 0x200 and sizeof(int) is 4, then p + 3 points to 0x20C, the start of the fourth element.
Key Takeaway

Think in elements not bytes: pointer arithmetic moves in element-sized steps.

Important comparison
Indexing and pointer arithmetic are two faces of the same operation; choose the one that improves readability while keeping performance identical.
Check your understanding
If you have int *r = matrix[row]; then r + col points to the element at row and col. Does r + 1 move to the next column or next row? Remember the pointer points to the row's first element.

screens.title: arr[i] vs *(arr + i)
screens.narratorSegment: Indexing with square brackets and dereferencing a computed pointer yield the same observable result. The expression arr[i] is defined by the language as equivalent to the dereference of arr plus i. That means both forms access the same address and read or write the same memory. A helpful mental model is to treat arr as the base address and then compute an offset. Using pointer arithmetic explicitly can clarify what is happening when you reason about addresses, while indexing often improves readability. A common beginner mistake is to assume arr always behaves like a mutable pointer variable; remember that arr in many contexts decays to a pointer but is not reassignable. Another useful symmetry is that i[arr] is also valid because the language defines it as *(i + arr). This oddity is rarely used in practice but demonstrates the underlying equivalence. Concrete example: printing an array's values using a for loop with arr[i] produces the same addresses and values as using *(arr + i) and printing the pointer address computed by arr + i. Try converting a simple loop both ways to confirm values and addresses match. Closing reflection: when would explicit pointer arithmetic help you spot a bug that indexing hides?

keyIdea.title: Equivalence
keyIdea.text: arr[i] is syntactic sugar for *(arr + i); both compute the same address and access the same element.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Indexing vs Dereference
Two equivalent forms
arr[i] and *(arr + i) produce the same effect: compute address then access value.
Readable form
Use arr[i] when clarity matters.
Explicit form
Use *(arr + i) when reasoning about address arithmetic or pointer traversal.
Quick example
/* conceptual */
int scores[] = {85,92,78};
// indexing
printf("%d at %p
", scores[1], (void*)&scores[1]);
// pointer arithmetic
printf("%d at %p
", *(scores + 1), (void*)(scores + 1));
Misconception check
Do not assume arr is a regular pointer you can assign to. The decay gives a pointer value in expressions but the array itself is not reassignable.
Try this

Convert a loop that uses arr[i] into one that advances a pointer and confirm the printed addresses match.

screens.title: Accessing Elements: Example Program
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a small program that prints array elements and addresses using both indexing and pointer arithmetic. The program defines an integer array, computes its size in the calling scope with sizeof, and then prints values and addresses using two loops. The important teaching point is that sizeof applied to the array in main gives the total bytes because the compiler knows the array length there. In contrast, once you pass the array to a function it decays to a pointer and sizeof inside the function returns the pointer size, not the array length. In the example you'll see scores plus i points to the same address printed when using &scores[i]. The code also shows assigning an int pointer to the array name—this is legal because the pointer receives the base address. However, trying to assign to the array name itself would be invalid. A common trap is to rely on sizeof inside a function to determine element count; always pass the length explicitly. To practice, run the program, inspect the printed addresses, and confirm that incrementing by one advances the address by sizeof(int) bytes. That exercise concretely links the theory of contiguity and pointer arithmetic to observable behavior.

keyIdea.title: Practical example
keyIdea.text: A worked program shows identical addresses and values for indexing and pointer arithmetic, and highlights sizeof differences across scopes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Example Program
Code
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
  int scores[] = {85, 92, 78, 95, 88};
  int size = sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]);

  printf("Indexing:
");
  for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
    printf("scores[%d] = %d at address %p
", i, scores[i], (void*)&scores[i]);
  }

  printf("
Pointer arithmetic:
");
  for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
    printf("*(scores + %d) = %d at address %p
", i, *(scores + i), (void*)(scores + i));
  }

  return 0;
}
Explanation
  • sizeof in main returns total bytes because the array size is known at compile time.
  • Both loops produce the same values and addresses — proof of equivalence.
  • Assigning int *ptr = scores; copies the base address into a pointer variable.
Common mistake

Do not use sizeof on a parameter inside a function to determine number of elements — the parameter is a pointer there.

Key Takeaway

Print addresses to confirm behavior: address increments match element sizes and confirm pointer/index equivalence.

screens.title: Multidimensional Arrays and Row-Major Order
screens.narratorSegment: Multidimensional arrays are arrays whose elements are themselves arrays. In C these are laid out in row-major order, meaning the entire first row is stored first, followed by the second row, and so on. For a 3 by 4 integer matrix this means matrix[0][0] through matrix[0][3] are contiguous, then matrix[1][0] through matrix[1][3], and so forth. That layout lets you compute any element's address using pointer arithmetic: the address of matrix[row][col] equals the base address plus (row times columns plus col) times sizeof(element). A common mistake is to assume column-major storage — languages differ — so you must know the language's ordering. Understanding row-major order is important when passing subarrays to functions or when flattening a matrix for linear algorithms. For access you can write *(*(matrix + row) + col) which is the pointer arithmetic equivalent of matrix[row][col]. As a concrete example, consider iterating a matrix row by row for cache-friendly access; because memory stores whole rows contiguously, row-major traversal yields better data locality. Reflect: when is it useful to treat a two-dimensional array as a single contiguous buffer? Multidimensional Arrays and Row-Major Order means multidimensional arrays are contiguous in row-major order: rows are stored sequentially, enabling flattened address computation.. In practical terms, how arrays of arrays map to contiguous memory. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Row-major layout
keyIdea.text: Multidimensional arrays are contiguous in row-major order: rows are stored sequentially, enabling flattened address computation.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Multidimensional Arrays
Row-major ordering
Rows are stored sequentially; each row's elements are contiguous.
Address formula
Address(matrix[row][col]) = base + ((row * columns) + col) * sizeof(element). Use this to compute offsets reliably.
Pointer form
matrix[row][col] equals *(*(matrix + row) + col). This emphasizes arrays of arrays with nested pointer arithmetic.
Key Takeaway

Treat multi-dimensional arrays as flattened buffers when computing addresses; row-major affects locality and traversal speed.

Example matrix layout (3 x 4)
Row 0: [m00][m01][m02][m03]
Row 1: [m10][m11][m12][m13]
Row 2: [m20][m21][m22][m23]
Performance note
Iterating row by row is cache friendly because consecutive accesses read adjacent memory locations.
Misconception
Do not assume column-major order; languages differ and assuming the wrong order leads to incorrect address calculations.

screens.title: Array Decay and Function Parameters
screens.narratorSegment: When you pass an array to a function in C, what is actually passed is a pointer to its first element. This is commonly called array decay: the array name decays into a pointer value in most expressions, including function calls. The practical consequence is that the function receives no copy of the elements; it receives a pointer that refers to the original memory. Because of that, any modification through the parameter affects the caller's array. Another critical consequence is that sizeof applied to the parameter inside the function yields the size of a pointer, not the array length. Beginners often expect sizeof inside the function to report the original array size, leading to off-by-one errors and incorrect loop bounds. The recommended pattern is to pass the array's length as a separate argument. For example, write int sumArray(int *arr_ptr, int count) and loop from zero to count. A useful contrast: declaring an array in main reserves a block; passing it hands over its start address. Ask yourself: which behaviors require explicit length information and which do not? The safe habit is to always carry size when passing arrays between scopes.

keyIdea.title: Array decay
keyIdea.text: Passing an array hands a pointer to its first element; the callee cannot determine element count from the parameter alone.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Array Decay
Decay: array name → pointer
The callee receives a pointer, not a copy of the array.
Pattern
Always pass length separately: int func(int *arr, int size).
Pitfall
sizeof(arr) inside a function gives pointer size. Do not use it to infer the number of elements.
Key Takeaway

Treat function parameters declared as arrays as pointers; include an explicit size parameter when needed.

Concrete example
int sumArray(int *arr_ptr, int count) {
  int sum = 0;
  for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    sum += *(arr_ptr + i);
  }
  return sum;
}
Notice that sizeof(arr_ptr) would print the pointer size, not the array's total bytes.

screens.title: Pass-by-Reference Example: sumArray and findMax
screens.narratorSegment: This exercise guides you to implement functions that operate on arrays through pointers. The first example sums elements by accepting an int pointer and a count, then uses pointer arithmetic to accumulate values. The second exercise is to complete a findMax function that returns the largest element found by traversing the array via the pointer. Important checks: handle size zero or negative size gracefully, and initialize your maximum value from the first element to avoid incorrect comparisons. A common error is to attempt to dereference a pointer without ensuring the array length is at least one — this leads to undefined behavior. Another pitfall is relying on a sentinel beyond the array bounds. A safe approach is to always pass the explicit number of elements and use a for loop that stops at the given length. After implementing these functions, test them by printing addresses and values in main using both indexing and pointer arithmetic to confirm behavior. Closing reflection: how does passing a pointer affect who owns the memory and when it may be freed or go out of scope?

screens.title: Buffer Overflow: Causes and Consequences
screens.narratorSegment: A buffer overflow happens when code writes data beyond the memory allocated for an array. Because arrays live adjacent to other memory regions, those extra writes overwrite other variables, control data, or heap metadata. Consequences can range from corrupted program state and crashes to security vulnerabilities where attackers exploit overwritten control data to change execution flow. Common causes include reading unbounded input into a fixed-size char buffer or failing to check loop bounds when copying arrays. To prevent overflow, always track the available size and use bounded library functions that accept a maximum length when manipulating strings or copying memory. For example, prefer functions that accept a destination size so you can ensure you never write more than allocated. Also adopt defensive programming: check indices before writing, and initialize buffers where appropriate. A helpful debugging technique is to print addresses and sizes during development to confirm your loops do not cross the known boundary. Final thought: correct bounds checking is simple but essential — making it a habit protects both program correctness and security. screens.title: Common Array and Pointer Errors
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners often make a small set of recurring errors when working with arrays and pointers. One is assuming the array name is an assignable pointer variable and trying to change it; the correct understanding is that the array's name is not a modifiable lvalue. Another is using sizeof inside a function parameter to compute element count — inside the function it measures pointer size, not array size. Off-by-one errors in loops are frequent: looping to the wrong bound writes past the last valid element. Also, failing to check for empty arrays before dereferencing the first element leads to undefined behavior. Finally, mixing pointer arithmetic with incorrect types produces incorrect addresses if you forget the element's size. To avoid these, adopt clear patterns: pass sizes explicitly, initialize values carefully, test edge cases like zero-length arrays, and prefer readable indexing for most code while using pointer arithmetic only when it clarifies the algorithm. Concrete practice: review a small function that receives int *arr and ensure it documents and validates the expected length before use. screens.title: Putting It Together: Trace and Test
screens.narratorSegment: When testing array and pointer code, adopt a repeatable routine: first, verify the declared sizes at the allocation site by computing element counts with sizeof when the array is visible. Second, when passing arrays to functions, ensure you also pass the length and validate it before use. Third, instrument small runs that print addresses and values for consecutive indices so you can confirm contiguity and correct pointer arithmetic. Fourth, include edge-case tests: empty arrays, single-element arrays, and maximum expected sizes. Finally, test unsafe inputs that try to overrun buffers and verify your bounds checks hold. A concrete practice task is to write a small main that prints each element's value and address using both indexing and pointer arithmetic, then call a function that sums elements using a pointer and explicit size. During debugging, printing addresses clarifies whether pointer arithmetic and indexing compute the same values. This routine builds confidence and reduces the chance of subtle bugs related to decay, sizeof surprises, or off-by-one loops. Closing question: which test case would reveal a mistaken assumption about array size inside a function?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will develop an intuitive picture of arrays and pointers in C and why they are tightly linked. Arrays are contiguous memory: elements sit next to each other so the address of one element directly leads to the next. That layout makes pointer arithmetic meaningful because moving a pointer moves by an element size, not by single bytes. You will learn the practical equivalence where an array name used in expressions becomes a pointer to its first element, what that decay means for assigning and for function calls, and why sizeof can mislead when used inside a function parameter. Along the way we will practice two ways to access elements — indexing and pointer arithmetic — and write small functions that accept arrays safely by receiving a pointer and a length. Finally, we will cover a critical safety topic: buffer overflows, why they happen when code writes past an array's bounds, and safer alternatives such as bounded copy functions. By the end you will be able to read and write array code with clearer expectations about addresses, performance, and safety, and answer practical questions such as why passing an array to a function does not copy all elements.

By the end of this chapter you will understand arrays as contiguous memory that stores elements of the same type, and you will be able to explain how array names commonly decay into pointers to their first element. You will learn to access elements with both array indexing and pointer arithmetic, and you will practice passing arrays to functions while correctly handling sizes because arrays decay into pointers at call sites. Finally, you will be able to identify and prevent common array-related errors, especially buffer overflows, by using bounds checks and safer library calls. For example, you will explain why giving a function just an array parameter does not preserve its original size and why you must pass a separate length. These skills let you write safer, clearer code that interoperates correctly with C APIs, and they form a foundation for working with multidimensional arrays and low-level memory reasoning.

This page frames the same learning goals in applied terms so you know what tasks show mastery. You will read and annotate a memory diagram to find addresses and offsets in a small integer array, and you will rewrite indexing access into pointer arithmetic to demonstrate equivalence. You will write functions that accept an array pointer and an explicit length parameter, then verify results by printing addresses to confirm decay. You will also complete a short program that finds the maximum element using pointer traversal to show pointer arithmetic in action. Finally, you will perform simple safety checks: never assume a function can compute an array's element count from a parameter alone, and always bound copies and reads. These practical checkpoints let you convert conceptual understanding into testable code behavior and reduce debugging time when memory issues appear.

An array is a fixed-size collection where elements of the same type occupy adjacent memory locations. Contiguous means no gaps: the address of element i plus one equals the address of element i plus the size of each element. That property is what enables efficient iteration, pointer arithmetic, and predictable address computation. For example, for an int array of five elements the compiler lays out five integer-sized slots in order so moving forward by one slot means advancing by the size of int on your platform. A common misconception is to treat an array name as a general-purpose pointer variable you can reassign; in C an array name often converts to a pointer in expressions but it is not a modifiable lvalue and cannot be assigned a new address. Another practical point: because memory is contiguous, traversing arrays with pointer arithmetic or indexing yields identical machine behavior, and the compiler can optimize linear scans effectively. Concrete example: if you declare int numbers[5]; the element numbers[3] resides at the address computed from numbers plus three times sizeof(int). Why this matters: understanding contiguity helps you predict performance, avoid accidental aliasing errors, and reason about how multi-dimensional arrays map to memory in row-major order. Try visualizing memory addresses as numbered slots; that mental model reveals how indexing and pointer math match perfectly.

Pointer arithmetic means the unit of pointer movement is the size of the pointed type. When you add one to an int pointer you advance by the number of bytes in an int on that platform. This behavior lets pointer expressions compute the address of any element: pointer plus index yields the correct memory location scaled by the element size. For example, if p points to an int array start, then p plus two points to the third int. A typical misunderstanding is thinking pointer addition moves by single bytes; it does not. The compiler scales the offset by sizeof(the pointed type). This scaling is what makes constructs like p plus i portable across platforms with different primitive sizes. Another practical note: you can both dereference the result of pointer addition and use indexing syntax — arr[i] is shorthand for *(arr + i). That identity helps you rewrite code for clarity or to practice pointer traversal in low-level loops. Example: walking a scores array with a loop that increments a pointer until it reaches the end uses the same element orders and yields identical values to an indexed loop. A closing question to try: if you have a pointer to row zero of a two-dimensional array, what does pointer plus one represent in terms of columns and rows?

Indexing with square brackets and dereferencing a computed pointer yield the same observable result. The expression arr[i] is defined by the language as equivalent to the dereference of arr plus i. That means both forms access the same address and read or write the same memory. A helpful mental model is to treat arr as the base address and then compute an offset. Using pointer arithmetic explicitly can clarify what is happening when you reason about addresses, while indexing often improves readability. A common beginner mistake is to assume arr always behaves like a mutable pointer variable; remember that arr in many contexts decays to a pointer but is not reassignable. Another useful symmetry is that i[arr] is also valid because the language defines it as *(i + arr). This oddity is rarely used in practice but demonstrates the underlying equivalence. Concrete example: printing an array's values using a for loop with arr[i] produces the same addresses and values as using *(arr + i) and printing the pointer address computed by arr + i. Try converting a simple loop both ways to confirm values and addresses match. Closing reflection: when would explicit pointer arithmetic help you spot a bug that indexing hides?

Let's walk through a small program that prints array elements and addresses using both indexing and pointer arithmetic. The program defines an integer array, computes its size in the calling scope with sizeof, and then prints values and addresses using two loops. The important teaching point is that sizeof applied to the array in main gives the total bytes because the compiler knows the array length there. In contrast, once you pass the array to a function it decays to a pointer and sizeof inside the function returns the pointer size, not the array length. In the example you'll see scores plus i points to the same address printed when using &scores[i]. The code also shows assigning an int pointer to the array name—this is legal because the pointer receives the base address. However, trying to assign to the array name itself would be invalid. A common trap is to rely on sizeof inside a function to determine element count; always pass the length explicitly. To practice, run the program, inspect the printed addresses, and confirm that incrementing by one advances the address by sizeof(int) bytes. That exercise concretely links the theory of contiguity and pointer arithmetic to observable behavior.

Multidimensional arrays are arrays whose elements are themselves arrays. In C these are laid out in row-major order, meaning the entire first row is stored first, followed by the second row, and so on. For a 3 by 4 integer matrix this means matrix[0][0] through matrix[0][3] are contiguous, then matrix[1][0] through matrix[1][3], and so forth. That layout lets you compute any element's address using pointer arithmetic: the address of matrix[row][col] equals the base address plus (row times columns plus col) times sizeof(element). A common mistake is to assume column-major storage — languages differ — so you must know the language's ordering. Understanding row-major order is important when passing subarrays to functions or when flattening a matrix for linear algorithms. For access you can write *(*(matrix + row) + col) which is the pointer arithmetic equivalent of matrix[row][col]. As a concrete example, consider iterating a matrix row by row for cache-friendly access; because memory stores whole rows contiguously, row-major traversal yields better data locality.
